extracted.intended_audience: aspiring authors, essayists, humorists, and cultivated conversationalists
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and standards for producing humorous/conversational essays, short stage pieces, and general social talk; covers how to write, how to proof and protect text, how to praise and criticize authors, and how to manage table-talk and private theatricals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insist on proofs and protect textual integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: “I am a very particular person about having all I write printed as I write it. I require to see a proof, a revise, a re-revise, and a double re-revise, or fourth-proof rectified impression of all my productions, especially verse. A misprint kills a sensitive author. An intentional change of his text murders him.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand to inspect successive proofs (proof, revise, re-revise, double re-revise) and resist editorial or committee alterations; consider charging for altered work (example: author charged committee double after their emendations). Misprints and unauthorized textual changes are severe harms to an author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Praise authors by appealing to emotion rather than calling them 'droll'
rubrics_metrics.description: “Be very careful how you tell an author he is _droll_. Ten to one he will hate you; and if he does, be sure he can do you a mischief... Say you _cried_ over his romance or his verses, and he will love you and send you a copy.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When complimenting writers, emphasize emotional reactions (e.g., say you 'cried' over their work) instead of labeling them merely funny or 'droll,' which may be resented and provoke hostility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversation should be suggestive rather than argumentative
rubrics_metrics.description: “Therefore conversation which is suggestive rather than argumentative, which lets out the most of each talker’s results of thought, is commonly the pleasantest and the most profitable.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor suggestiveness, implication, and the sharing of impressions over blunt disputation. Let each speaker reveal their thoughts; cultivate talk as an artistic product rather than a forensic contest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow embellishment, partial truths, and artistic exaggeration in talk
rubrics_metrics.description: “Neither make too much of flaws and occasional overstatements. ... conversation must have its partial truths, its embellished truths, its exaggerated truths. It is in its higher forms an artistic product... One man who is a little too literal can spoil the talk of a whole tableful of men of _esprit_.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept and even use tasteful exaggeration and figurative speech in conversation; avoid spoiling the effect by over-literal correction. If someone is excessively literal or paradoxical in a damaging way, a well-placed factual correction ('stick a fact into him like a stiletto') may be warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand wit as a partial, selective view (not total truth)
rubrics_metrics.description: “There is a perfect consciousness in every form of wit... that its essence consists in a partial and incomplete view of whatever it touches. It throws a single ray, separated from the rest... We get beautiful effects from wit,—all the prismatic colors,—but never the object as it is in fair daylight.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that wit highlights one facet of a subject for effect; it is not meant to give the whole truth. Avoid mistaking cleverness for comprehensive insight; use wit deliberately as a selective lens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise tact with intimates; friendship does not license frank rudeness
rubrics_metrics.description: “Don’t flatter yourselves that friendship authorizes you to say disagreeable things to your intimates. On the contrary, the nearer you come into relation with a person, the more necessary do tact and courtesy become.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume intimacy gives carte blanche to speak harshly; preserve amour-propre and be courteous. Where necessary, allow unpleasant truths to come from others rather than inflicting them yourself.

rubrics_metrics.name: High conversation relies on shared assumptions — take much for granted
rubrics_metrics.description: “The whole force of conversation depends on how much you can take for granted... Just so in talking with first-rate men; especially when they are good-natured and expansive, as they are apt to be at table.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In cultivated or high-level talk, rely on shared background and implicit understanding so that complex points can be compressed (illustrated by 'Mate in six moves'). Cultivate interlocutors who share assumptions so conversation can move by implication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid exhausting your best material in a first novel
rubrics_metrics.description: “An author’s first novel is naturally drawn, to a great extent, from his personal experiences... But the moment the author gets out of his personality, he must have the creative power... Besides, there is great danger that a man’s first life-story shall clean him out, so to speak, of his best thoughts.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about pouring all your most vivid personal experiences and best thoughts into an initial work; preserve reserves of material and cultivate imaginative/creative resources beyond literal autobiography if you intend a sustained career.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect friends from being exposed in fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: “Again, I am terribly afraid I should show up all my friends... I am afraid all my friends would not bear showing up very well; for they have an average share of the common weakness of humanity, which I am pretty certain would come out.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drawing on real people in stories, avoid identifying or caricaturing acquaintances in ways that would embarrass them; exercise discretion to prevent harming relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Send manuscripts to impartial editors rather than relying on relatives' judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: “So never mind what your cousins, brothers, sisters, uncles, aunts, and the rest, say about that fine poem you have written, but send it (postage-paid) to the editors, if there are any, of the ‘Atlantic’... Strangers are commonly the first to find the ‘gift’ that came with the little book.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not depend on relatives’ praise or critiques; submit work to professional/independent editors and publishers, who are likelier to recognize merit. Pay postage and present your work properly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer natural, unexaggerated acting in private theatricals
rubrics_metrics.description: “Private theatricals, as I have figured in them in country lyceum-halls, are one thing,—and private theatricals, as they may be seen in certain gilded and frescoed saloons of our metropolis, are another. ... it is pleasant to see real gentlemen and ladies, who do not think it necessary to mouth, and rant, and stride, like most of our stage heroes and heroines... most of all to see a fresh, unrouged, unspoiled, high bred young maiden... acting in those love-dramas which make us young again to look upon.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor restrained, natural performance over overacting (mouthing, ranting, striding). In private/amateur productions, modest, fresh portrayals are most effective; avoid theatrical excesses that call attention to artifice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle literary thieves and pretentiousness with measured ridicule rather than vindictive exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: “I once read an introductory lecture that looked to me too learned for its latitude. On examination, I found all its erudition was taken ready-made from D’Israeli... one can generally tell these wholesale thieves easily enough, and they are not worth the trouble of putting them in the pillory.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When encountering plagiarism or sham erudition, identify it if useful but avoid making a public vendetta; measured exposure or quiet disdain is often preferable to elaborate pillorying.

rubrics_metrics.name: A cultivated conversational environment (club or reader) magnifies the value of speech
rubrics_metrics.description: “A Club is the next best thing to this, strung like a harp, with about a dozen ringing intelligences, each answering to some chord of the macrocosm. ... If _I_ were a prince, I would hire or buy a private literary tea-pot, in which I would steep all the leaves of new books that promised well... a quick-witted, out-spoken, incisive fellow... knows all the common plots... can give you a criticism of an octavo in an epithet and a wink.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To elevate one's conversation and critical appreciation, cultivate or join a circle of informed interlocutors or employ a knowledgeable reader/critic who can distill and present literary substance; these arrangements let you enjoy distilled cultural capital without exhaustive reading yourself.
